section_summary: This section opens with the continuation of an extensive report on Japanese occupation policies in China, including educational control, economic plunder, resource exploitation, smuggling, blockade, rationing, puppet banks and currency warfare, together with proposed Chinese countermeasures. It then contains Stockholm and Bern reporting on Mitsui expansion, Japanese economic relations with Thailand and the Philippines, wartime clothing, Manchurian industry and the conversion of Japanese factories to war-related production. The final documents record State Department deliberations and a lengthy draft policy for the postwar economic control of Japan, covering disarmament, minimum economic relief, restitution, reparations and control of Japan's war potential.

subfiles.title: Japanese political, economic and currency aggression in occupied China (continued)
subfiles.about: Continuation of a report describing Japanese political and economic control in occupied China and recommending Chinese countermeasures.
subfiles.summary: The fragment concludes a discussion of Japanese-controlled education, propaganda and pacification before turning to the tactics of economic warfare. It details direct plunder, resource exploitation, smuggling, dumping, blockade and rationing, including the corporations, commercial firms and administrative machinery used to control occupied territory. A subsequent chapter explains puppet banks, military yen, Federal Reserve and Central Reserve Bank notes, the suppression and counterfeiting of Chinese National Currency and Chinese defensive measures. The report proposes unified government purchasing operations, economic police, tighter counter-blockades and banking measures to recover materials and absorb currency near the front.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3965: Japanese Economic Items Reported by the German Press
subfiles.from: Herschel V. Johnson, American Legation, Stockholm
subfiles.about: Transmits a Legation memorandum summarizing German press reports on Japanese economic conditions and colonial policies.
subfiles.summary: Johnson forwards a memorandum prepared by the Legation's Foreign Countries Division from recent issues of the Krakauer Zeitung. He identifies four subjects: Mitsui expansion, Japanese economic collaboration with Thailand, agricultural readjustment in the Philippines and standardized clothing in Japan. Copies were also directed to the political and economic-warfare divisions of the American Embassy in London.

subfiles.title: Certain Aspects of Japanese Economic Life and Colonial Aspirations
subfiles.from: Foreign Countries Division, American Legation, Stockholm
subfiles.about: Summarizes August 1944 Krakauer Zeitung articles on Japanese industry, colonial economic cooperation, Philippine agriculture and civilian clothing.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reports the capitalization and expansion of Mitsui mining and chemical enterprises, including synthetic-fuel production and the anticipated exploitation of occupied Asian mineral resources. It describes Japanese assistance to and exploitation of Thailand through joint industries, banking, shipping, teak and rice production. It also discusses Japanese-directed conversion of Philippine sugar and cotton land to rice cultivation. A final section describes clothing rationing, women's mompei trousers, men's standard Kokumin Yofuku suits and identification badges bearing names, addresses and blood groups.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3965: Japanese Economic Items Reported by the German Press (file copy)
subfiles.from: Herschel V. Johnson, American Legation, Stockholm
subfiles.about: Stamped file copy of the despatch transmitting German press summaries concerning the Japanese economy.
subfiles.summary: This is a duplicate departmental copy of the despatch on page 63. It repeats the description of the four enclosed subjects and bears later Department of State routing and reproduction stamps.

subfiles.title: Certain Aspects of Japanese Economic Life and Colonial Aspirations (file copy)
subfiles.from: Foreign Countries Division, American Legation, Stockholm
subfiles.about: Duplicate enclosure summarizing German newspaper reports on Japanese economic and colonial developments.
subfiles.summary: This file copy duplicates the memorandum on pages 64-66. It covers Mitsui mining and chemicals, Japanese-Thai industrial and financial cooperation, Japanese agricultural planning in the Philippines and wartime clothing standardization in Japan.

subfiles.title: CAC 160, “Japan: Economic Policy”
subfiles.about: Reports committee debate over proposed amendments to the American economic-policy paper on Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Interdivisional Committee on the Far East reopened CAC 160 after suggestions from FMA and the ECA Committee. Members disputed whether policy toward Japan should conform to German economic-policy documents or instead rest on circumstances particular to Japan and established American policy and international law. Chairman Blakeslee concluded that the policies need not be identical, while discussion of using private property for reparations ended without a decision.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 5789, Second: Japanese Economic Developments
subfiles.about: Reports published information on Manchurian heavy industry and Japanese factory conversions.
subfiles.summary: The telegram states that Manchurian iron and steel capacity had reached roughly half that of Japan proper and that rising industrial coal demand had turned Manchuria from an exporter into an importer of North Chinese coking coal. It reports the conversion of cotton and rayon factories to chemicals, aircraft parts, machinery, fuels and other war-related production. It also describes efforts to convert surplus soda-industry equipment to magnesium chloride and alumina production.

subfiles.title: Economic Policy toward Japan
subfiles.from: C. F. Remer and Oliver C. Lockhart, FMA
subfiles.about: Forwards two proposed versions of American economic policy toward Japan and outlines a phased control mechanism.
subfiles.summary: The authors submit alternative policy statements for discussion within ECA and later presentation to the Far Eastern Area Committee. They recommend immediate military economic control with civilian advisers, followed by a civilian commission with military advisers and a reparations subcommission. They propose ending the commission when close supervision and reparations cease, with no control commission during the third period.

subfiles.title: Postwar American Economic Policy Toward Japan
subfiles.about: Drafts the objectives, phases and instruments of American economic policy for defeated postwar Japan.
subfiles.summary: The paper grounds policy in peace, Chinese sovereignty, equal commercial opportunity and the removal of Japan's capacity for renewed aggression. It interprets the Cairo decisions as requiring the loss of Korea, Formosa, Pacific islands and control over Manchuria, while advocating equal economic relations between Japan and its former dependencies. Three periods are proposed: disarmament and maintenance of a minimum economy, close economic control with reparations, and gradual reintegration into the world economy. The draft calls for relief, transportation and financial services, inflation control, restitution of stolen property, seizure of appropriate overseas assets and reparations from stocks, equipment and current production, with payments ending within ten years. Its final pages begin a discussion of controlling Japan's economic war potential through destruction, dismantling, conversion or scrapping of war plants.
